title: SQL Indexes & Query Plans
oneLiner: Why the same query takes 0.1 ms or 10 ms, and how to ask the database which one you're going to get.
keyTakeaway: An index is a sorted copy of one or more columns with pointers back to the rows -- a binary search tree for your table. It turns "read every row" (a SCAN, O(n)) into "jump to the matches" (a SEARCH, O(log n)). It isn't free: every INSERT, UPDATE and DELETE has to keep every index up to date, so index the columns you actually filter and join on, not everything.
explanation:
Without an index, `WHERE customer_id = 42` has exactly one strategy: read every row in the table and keep the ones that match. On 200 rows nobody notices. On 200,000 rows it's the difference between a page that loads instantly and one that doesn't, and it gets worse every day the table grows.

An index fixes that the same way a book's index does. `CREATE INDEX idx_orders_customer ON orders(customer_id)` builds a separate structure (a B-tree, a wide, shallow cousin of the binary search tree from the Trees track) holding every customer_id in sorted order, each pointing back at its row. Finding customer 42 becomes a binary-search-style descent instead of a full read. The primary key already works this way, which is why lookups by id are always fast.

You don't have to guess whether an index is used: put `EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN` (SQLite) or `EXPLAIN` (PostgreSQL, MySQL; SQL Server shows an execution plan) in front of the query. `SCAN orders` means a full read; `SEARCH orders USING INDEX ...` means the index did its job. Reading plans is the single most useful habit for fixing a slow query.

Three things that catch people out, all in the presets below. Column order in a composite index (one index over several columns) matters: an index on (customer_id, created_at) is sorted by customer first, so it helps "customer 42 since June" but not "everyone since June". Wrapping the column in a function (`WHERE lower(status) = ...`) hides it from the index. And every index makes writes slower, since each INSERT has to update every index too -- the "Time 20,000 inserts" button shows the cost.
